messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At 69, Linda had spent most of her adult life doing seasonal agricultural work, the kind of labor that organized her days by weather, harvest, and the routines of the same rural roads. She was married and had always thought of herself as practical, someone who endured hard things by keeping moving. The assault happened after a long workday when she was waiting for a bus ride home, tired and alone, and a man she did not know forced himself on her. In the months since, the details had not settled into the past. They returned suddenly and without warning, not as a story she could choose to tell, but as a memory that cut into the present with the same bodily jolt and shame. Bus riding became especially potent because the bus stop, the enclosed space, and the feeling of being trapped with strangers all belonged to what happened.

Afterward, Linda found that ordinary moments could set everything off. If she had to take public transport for work, or even saw a bus pull up along the road, the memory could come into her mind with such force that she felt she was right back there. Certain conversation topics—especially when other workers spoke casually about sex, safety, or men behaving badly—could bring the same sudden rush. When this happened, she tried to get through it the only ways that seemed to offer any relief: she drank in the evenings, sometimes took medication to dull herself, and increasingly kept away from other people. She also began mentally rehearsing worst case scenarios before leaving home, telling herself that if she imagined every possible danger she might be less helpless next time.

Those same triggers also changed the way she moved through the world. A bus passing her in town, a coworker starting the wrong kind of conversation, or a memory arriving out of nowhere could leave her scanning immediately, looking behind her to make sure no one was following. She had come to feel safe only in a very limited set of places—her house, one corner of the fields where she could see in every direction, her husband’s truck. Outside those zones, fear, anger, shame, and a sickened sense of exposure came on fast. What frightened her most was how quickly the feeling took over, as if the danger were not over at all but still waiting just outside her line of sight.

The triggers also fed the way she had started to think about herself. Each time she froze on a bus route or felt her stomach drop when a conversation turned, Linda took it as proof that she could not rely on herself anymore. She had once trusted her own judgment, and now she questioned whether she could keep herself safe even in ordinary situations. Around coworkers she increasingly felt set apart, as though everyone else still belonged to the everyday world and she had been pushed outside it. The sudden intrusions made her feel marked and isolated, different in a way she believed would never fully go away.

Over time, those beliefs hardened and began shaping what she did. Because she felt she could not rely on herself, she leaned more heavily on alcohol and pills to get through nights and to quiet herself before bus rides she could not avoid. Because she felt like an outsider, avoiding people began to seem sensible rather than sad; staying away spared her the strain of pretending to be normal. Worst case rehearsal also fit with that view of herself—if she was no longer the kind of person who could trust her instincts in the moment, then she felt she had to plan obsessively in advance for everything that might happen.

Those same beliefs made the triggers sharper. When a memory surfaced, it did not remain just a memory; it immediately confirmed for Linda that she was damaged, alone, and no longer capable of managing as she once had. Even overhearing certain topics at work could sting with more than recollection, because she was already primed to hear herself as separate from other people. In that state, she noticed buses more quickly, heard snippets of conversation more intensely, and seemed to brace for the memory before it even arrived.

Her constant vigilance tightened this further. Because she was always checking behind her and measuring where safety might still exist, the world became full of reminders. Bus stops, crowded aisles, and loose talk among workers stood out to her more than they once would have. The more she scanned for danger, the more easily the intrusive memory broke through. And the ways she coped kept narrowing her life. Avoiding people left her with fewer distractions and more room for the memory to intrude. Drinking and medication blurred the evenings but seemed to leave her more brittle the next day, while all the rehearsing of worst case scenarios kept her mind close to threat, so that even before dawn shifts in the fields she was already tense and looking over her shoulder.

She finally sought help after realizing how small her life had become. She had started refusing some transport-dependent work, withdrawing from coworkers, and relying on her husband for errands she once handled herself. What she fears most is that this is permanent—that she will remain an outsider in her own life, unable to trust herself, safe only in a shrinking set of places. What she hopes, though she says it cautiously, is to be able to ride where she needs to go, hear ordinary conversation without unraveling, and feel that the assault is no longer happening every day.
